interest and against justice, and for the purpose of oppressing an 
individual; such a prosecution would not be a faithful execution of 
the law; and upon the President being satisfied that the forms of 
law were abused for such a purpose, and being bound to take care 
that the law was faithfully executed, it would become his duty to 
take measures to correct the procedure. And the most natural and 
proper measure to accomphsh that object would be, to order the 
district attorney to discontinue the prosecution. The district 
attorney might refuse to obey the President’s order; and if he did 
refuse, the prosecution, while he remained in office, would still go 
on; because the President could give no order to the court or the 
clerk to make any particular entry. He could only act through his 
subordinate officer, the district attorney, who is responsible to 
him, and who holds his office at his pleasure. And if that officer 
still continued a prosecution which the President was satisfied 
ought to be discontinued, the removal of the disobedient officer, 
and the substitution of one more worthy in his place, would enable 
the President, through him, faithfully to execute the law. And it 
is for this, among other reasons, that the power of removing the 
district attorney resides in the President. * * *
The Jewels of the Princess of Orange, 2 Op. A.G. 482 (1831). Note that the 
case that Taney hypothesizes for appropriate presidential intervention—a 
case in which the president determines that a prosecution would be 
“against Justice”—^is not described as a case in which prosecution would be 
unlawful. Taney thus seems not only to disagree with Wirt about the 
president’s entitlement to direct a subordinate in the exercise of a duty 
conferred on that subordinate by statute, but he also implies that, in 
guiding his subordinates, the president may issue directives based on his 
policy judgments as well.
Here, as elsewhere, a sound interpretation of past practice requires 
attention to the political and institutional context surrounding legal 
disagreement. Wirt was a Jeffersonian Republican serving a president who 
(whatever his own practices) consistently articulated a restrained view of 
presidential power and was answering a question about a treasury officer 
exercising what might be considered “quasi-judicial” functions. Taney 
served a president intent on flexing the fullest possible powers of the 
presidency—Jackson was lampooned in the press as “King Andrew” and 
was censured by the Senate for executive overreaching—and was 
responding to a question concerning prosecution by a U.S. Attorney who 
was at the time not subject to any effective departmental supervision. 
(Congress did not create the Justice Department until 1870.)
